I don't see this mentioned anywhere, but I believe we're missing a T.

First we had T for Training, where we provided huge amounts of data to let an algorithm create an artificial neural network model.

Now we have T for Test-time-compute, allowing a model to finetune its output.

But we overlooked T for Teaching, where WE (as a collective human society) fact check and correct the AI's produced output, then letting the model incorporate that new data (by intermediate training), consequently aligning the model with how the real world works, how humans think, and eventually even enabling it try and understand the human species.

Training itself is what a new born baby does. (AI)
Years of Teaching is what a child and teenager receives, practising learning to think. (AGI?).
Thinking (Test-time-compute) is what a graduate does (ASI??).

How to decide what to teach AI? I don't know. Maybe an improved method that's based on the Community Notes system, with a non binding bias towards the opinion of established specialists, voted on by that same community? Again, I don't really know :)

comments.text:
I think you're overgeneralizing with that curve. The leap forward shown was gained by adding basically one new technique to what LLMs already did—and one that it was fairly obvious LLMs needed—which improved AI in one category of test that it was bad at before.  The Arc test designer himself has said that it's still pretty easy to come up with tests that are easy for most humans and hard or impossible for ai. So another way to look at this would be: if a breakthrough like the one we recently saw turns out to be needed for each of many categories of human intelligence, then no, we're not approaching AGI or ASI at an exponential rate. 

I really like the chart that google produced 20:00 because it's clear in what it's intended to convey. At each tier, consider an AI that is smart as this example is in this one arena, but it's that smart in all arenas. So is Arc an arena, rather than a valid canary for AGI? It's just one type of problem that humans are or were better at than AI. We don't know how "general" the new models are. 

Even if we generalize to "reasoning," that's still only slice of what humans do with their brains. There's creativity. Our ability to interpret and convey subtle nuance. Intuitive hunches. (I don't mean that in a woo sense, I mean it in the sense of valid, useful mental processes that aren't based in reasoning or rational thought.) Not to mention humor, emotions, empathy, ...

Check out Adam Neely's video on what it would take for an AI to sit in on a Jazz jam session—all the layers of complex cognitive skills that come into play. Few if any of which are demonstrated by o1, o3, or any other AIs. But which are just special cases of typical cognitive abilities for humans.
